title: Deterministic Verification and a Single‑Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a sealed, preregistered paired experiment that measured the marginal verifier-detected effect of interposing a deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial generation call per intent; that identical candidate reused for both baseline and guarded episodes) we generated one candidate per natural-language intent with gpt-5-mini for N = 250 pairs and evaluated two episodes per intent: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if failing, permit one automated repair). Execution completed 500 episodes with model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial-generation + 1 repair). Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); contingency n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; paired difference (guarded − baseline) = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted repair. Important confirmatory-scope note (preregistration deviation): the preregistered sim‑to‑real/production-like confirmatory contrast was not executed; the reported confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition executed in this run. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced in the condensed Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being explored as intent‑to‑configuration translators in network operations (NetOps), promising faster authoring of device CLI sequences and intent‑driven automation. Stochastic generation, however, creates operational risk: syntax errors, incorrect command ordering, local‑policy violations, and vendor‑CLI subtleties can produce unsafe or non‑functional device changes. Prior empirical and survey work demonstrates LLM feasibility for producing draft configurations in controlled settings while noting the continuing need for deterministic verification or human oversight [1],[2].

A common architectural response interposes a deterministic validator between generation and acceptance, optionally followed by bounded automated repair — a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pattern — which accepts only validator‑passed candidates or attempts limited repair when mechanically verifiable defects are detected [3],[4]. GVR pipelines reduce mechanically checkable error classes (syntax, ordering, local policy), yet it remains unclear how large the marginal verifier/repair benefit is when a capable LLM already produces well‑formed candidates under constrained task regimes.

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑backed paired experiment that isolates the marginal validator+single‑repair effect when the same initial candidate is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). By design the experiment measures only the validator‑and‑repair marginal effect on identical model outputs rather than conflating generation variability across conditions. Our contribution is an artifact‑grounded quantification of that marginal verifier effect (counts, exact paired test, bootstrap CI), explicit provider‑call reconciliation, and an audit‑friendly record of validator traces and repair activity.
sections.related_work:
Recent NetOps and LLM surveys, benchmarks, and system reports show active work on intent‑to‑config translation, GVR architectures, and deterministic validators. Representative empirical and survey studies find that (a) LLMs can produce usable draft configurations in controlled or emulation settings but often require verification or human oversight [1],[2]; (b) deterministic configuration analyzers and model‑checking tools (e.g., Batfish and related header‑space approaches) are mature mechanisms for mechanized checks used as validators in research pipelines [3],[5]; and (c) generate–and–verify or generate–repair workflows improve detection and correction for mechanically verifiable defects in code and configuration domains, though deeper semantic correctness and cross‑vendor subtleties remain challenging [4],[6].

Security literature on prompt‑injection and retrieval threats documents realistic attack vectors against LLM‑integrated applications and motivates filtering, detection, and validation layers for operational deployments [7]. Our study differs from prior work by (i) freezing a preregistered paired estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics that isolates only validator/repair marginal effects on identical candidates, (ii) providing explicit provider‑call and stage‑count reconciliation, and (iii) archiving deterministic validator traces and repair artifacts for audit.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. We preregistered study‑id study‑cand‑2026‑LLM‑verifier‑sim2real‑v1, a confirmatory paired design with N_pairs = 250, generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate, a single allowed automated repair per episode, preregistered exclusion/contamination rules, and the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration SHA‑256 is 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede and is archived with the evidence bundle.

Explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics and provider‑call accounting (clarification). Per the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design, for each intent we produced exactly one initial model‑generation call; that identical generated candidate (the "shared initial") was reused for both episodes belonging to the pair: baseline (accept candidate) and guarded (run deterministic validation; if validation fails, permit up to one automated repair attempt). No independent first‑pass generation was made per condition. Provider‑call reconciliation in the adapter audit records hosted_model_call_event_count = 251 which decomposes deterministically to 250 shared initial_generation calls plus 1 repair call (model_calls_used = 251). Adapter labels in the audit use condition_counts = {"shared": 250, "guarded": 1} because the adapter records the shared initial generation events under the "shared" label and the single repair call under the label used for the repair stage; stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1} provides the explicit per‑stage mapping. This paragraph is intended to remove ambiguity about the adapter labels and to make the decomposition and shared_initial_candidate semantics explicit for readers.

Task generation and constraints. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 250 constrained intents. Each manifest entry encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and a difficulty label (medium/hard/very_hard). Tasks exercised typical NetOps workflow constraints (make‑before‑break uplink switchover, paired‑link atomic MTU changes, controlled VLAN migrations) and protected interfaces. Representative task payloads and the full manifest are archived in the evidence bundle.

Model and guarded pipeline. The declared model for all initial generations was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json record). For each pair: (1) call model once to produce the shared candidate; (2) baseline episode accepts the shared candidate and records validator outcome under the baseline scoring channel; (3) guarded episode submits the shared candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator parses CLI sequences, counts parsed_command_count, checks required_sequence ordering and workflow constraints, snapshots the implied final_state, and returns a boolean valid flag plus violation details. If valid = false in a guarded episode the pipeline may perform one deterministic template‑driven repair (reordering commands, splitting/joining tokens, minor syntactic fixes) and resubmit once to the validator. Repair templates were restricted to deterministic, non‑creative transformations; multi‑iteration or free‑form repairs and human escalation were not permitted by design.

Inclusion, contamination, and missingness rules. The preregistered exclusions removed items that deterministically prevented validation (vendor‑parser failure), contained credential‑like tokens or denylist matches, or raised deterministic verifier runtime errors; contamination detectors flagged instruction‑like embedded tokens or private addresses. The preregistered missingness treatment excluded such items from the primary confirmatory analysis and enumerated sensitivity analyses. In the executed confirmatory partition no episodes were excluded or flagged; complete_pair_count = 250.

Confirmatory analysis. The primary analysis used a paired binary analysis with an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). All analysis code and the contingency table are archived.
sections.results:
Execution and counts. Execution completed the preregistered confirmatory partition with planned_episode_count = 500 and completed_episode_count = 500 (250 pairs). Model_call accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair). No episodes were excluded for contamination or parser failures.

Primary binary outcomes and contingency. Validator‑scored successes: baseline_success_count = 249 (baseline_success_rate = 0.996), guarded_success_count = 250 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Observed paired contingency: n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The single discordant pair (baseline failed, guarded passed) corresponds to the sole exercised repair call; the repair‑conversion rate on the confirmatory partition is 1/250 = 0.4%.

Statistical inference and uncertainty. Exact McNemar (two‑sided) on discordant counts (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) returns p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the guarded − baseline paired difference (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.012] (0–1.2 percentage points). These results and the bootstrap parameters are preserved in the analysis artifacts.

Validator diagnostics and representative traces. Passed episodes show parsed_command_count equal to the task required_command_count and validator final_state snapshots that match the manifest expected_final_state. Representative scoring artifacts (for example task‑000003) demonstrate correct parsing, the expected number of commands, and valid = true in both baseline and guarded channels. The single repair trace shows a deterministic reorder/fix that converted a failing candidate into a validator pass; that repair trace and its guarded scoring artifact are archived.

Missingness and contamination. analysis/missingness_summary reports complete_pairs = 250 and all missingness counts = 0. Contamination detectors flagged no confirmatory episodes; analysis/contamination_summary is empty.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the near‑null marginal effect. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the constrained synthetic/emulation partition used here, the marginal verifier‑detected benefit of inserting a deterministic validator plus a single automated repair was small: initial gpt‑5‑mini candidates satisfied the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the single permitted repair converted the only failing candidate. The paired‑bootstrap CI upper bound (1.2 percentage points) empirically bounds the verifier‑improvement under these study conditions.

Artifact‑grounded factors explaining the small observed gain. Three artifact‑grounded factors likely produced the observed small marginal gain: (1) the deterministic task generator encoded constrained intents and allowed_touched_fields that reduced ambiguity and favored well‑formed CLI sequences; (2) the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) produced highly consistent, syntactically well‑formed sequences for these constrained intents; and (3) the deterministic validator checks mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, ordering, expected_final_state snapshots) but does not capture live protocol‑level correctness or emergent cross‑device interactions.

Power, assumptions, and practical meaning. The preregistration power calculation assumed a baseline pass rate ≈ 0.90 and targeted detection of a 15 percentage‑point absolute effect with ≈80% power using N_pairs = 250. The observed baseline pass rate (0.996) is substantially higher than assumed, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements; therefore the bootstrap CI and the exact counts provide the most informative practical bounds for this task bank. These results do not imply validators or repairs are unnecessary in broader or adversarial contexts; different task scopes, looser intent encodings, multi‑iteration repairs, richer validators, or production heterogeneity could yield larger marginal benefits.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: dependence on prompt templates, repair template design, the single‑repair policy, and the explicit shared_initial_candidate design. Construct validity: the deterministic validator measures mechanically verifiable correctness (syntax, sequence, snapshot) but not full operational semantics or runtime protocol dynamics. External validity: the confirmatory evidence covers only the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production‑like partitions were not executed in this run. Security: adaptive prompt‑injection and retrieval‑based adversaries were not exercised and remain open risks.

Reproducibility and auditability. Key reconciliation facts reported above (model_calls_used = 251, stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1}, contingency counts n11 = 249 / n10 = 1 / n01 = 0 / n00 = 0, bootstrap parameters) are reproducible from the archived manifests and analysis CSVs. For compactness we provide a single evidence pointer in the Disclosure Statement to the archived run artifacts that include the full manifests, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis outputs.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier‑detected marginal benefit of deterministic validation plus one permitted automated repair on identical LLM‑generated configuration candidates. In N = 250 constrained synthetic intent tasks initial gpt‑5‑mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases; the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate via the single permitted repair. Observed paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp]; p = 1.0). We explicitly disclose that the preregistered sim‑to‑real confirmatory contrast was not executed and that the executed confirmatory estimand applies only to the synthetic/emulation partition. Broader production, adversarial, multi‑model, and multi‑iteration repair evaluations remain necessary to establish generality. All execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts referenced in this paper are archived and available in the evidence bundle described in the Disclosure Statement.

disclosure_statement:
Human role and autonomy boundary: After the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher autonomy lock, the autonomous system performed literature search, study selection, preregistration freeze, model calls, deterministic validation, permitted repair execution, analysis, drafting, peer‑review, revision, and finalization without manual human editing of technical content. A human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and performed pre‑lock infrastructure development only; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.

Models, tools, and single manifest pointer: Declared model = gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). Deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Deterministic task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration study id = study‑cand‑2026‑LLM‑verifier‑sim2real‑v1 (preregistration SHA‑256: 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede). Immutable master prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. A compact pointer into the archived execution/analysis bundle is provided here for audit: execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 438fa6fa665160f917f0da85021f6e3102c9fcbc38a76fb5d6187f3a58d150d9). The archive contains the full execution manifest, task manifest, provider‑call audit, deterministic reconciliation, validator traces, repair traces, analysis CSVs (including the paired contingency), and other artifacts referenced in this manuscript.

Executed estimand and confirmed deviation: The preregistration included synthetic/emulation, community, and production‑like partitions and planned a sim‑to‑real confirmatory contrast. Deviation disclosure (explicit): the preregistered sim‑to‑real/production‑like confirmatory contrast was not executed in this run; the executed confirmatory estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated on the synthetic/emulation partition only (N_pairs = 250; shared_initial_candidate semantics). Provider‑call accounting reconciles to model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial_generation + 1 repair) and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 250, "repair": 1} as archived. No manual manuscript edits of technical content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Confirmatory scope limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; preregistered community and production‑like partitions were not executed and remain exploratory.

Deterministic validator assessed mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences) but did not measure broader semantic or behavioral correctness (protocol dynamics, emergent interactions).
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi‑model or alternate‑validator generality.
Only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi‑iteration repairs or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation were not evaluated.
Adversarial and retrieval‑based attacks (adaptive prompt‑injection, vendor‑targeted exploit vectors) and large‑scale production heterogeneity were not exercised and remain open threats.
